# Physics 11 — implementation plan

Source: CDC Nepal, Grade 11 Physics, feedback copy, 2024. All 26 chapters are mapped below; original numbering is preserved.

78 laboratories use shared parameter state for controls, equations, live prose, calculations, Canvas scenes and parameter graphs. React components manage shared state and Pretext lays out Canvas explanations. Analytical physics is appropriate here; Rapier is unnecessary for the scoped models.

| Chapter / printed page | Implemented labs | Reading and model limits |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Physical quantities / p.1 | Speed and units (v (m/s) = v (km/h) ÷ 3.6); Area and uncertainty (A = lb; ΔA ≈ bΔl + lΔb); Build a dimension ([Q] = Mᵃ Lᵇ Tᶜ) | Definitions and measurement history stay as reading. Dimensional consistency does not determine numerical constants. Real instrument calibration requires a physical instrument. |
| 2. Vectors / p.21 | Vector addition (R = √(A² + B² + 2AB cos θ)); Resolve a vector (Aₓ = A cos θ; Aᵧ = A sin θ); Dot product (A · B = AB cos θ) | Vector definitions and proofs remain readable. The lab uses a two-dimensional coordinate plane; three-dimensional generalization is described by the same component rules. |
| 3. Kinematics / p.41 | Constant acceleration (s = ut + ½at²; v = u + at); Projectile laboratory (Range = u² sin(2θ) / g); Relative velocity (v relative = v₁ − v₂) | The constant-acceleration and projectile models do not describe air resistance. Timing a real moving object remains a hands-on task. |
| 4. Dynamics / p.73 | Newton’s second law (a = F net / m); Friction on a slope (a = 0 if tan θ ≤ μₛ; otherwise g(sin θ − μₖ cos θ)); Turning effect (τ = rF sin θ) | Newton’s laws and conservation arguments need reasoning. The incline model distinguishes static and kinetic friction; real surfaces may not follow constant coefficients. |
| 5. Work, energy & power / p.103 | Work at an angle (W = Fs cos θ); Energy and power (Eₖ = ½mv²; P average = Eₖ / t); A sticking collision (v final = (m₁u₁ + m₂u₂) / (m₁ + m₂)) | Energy bookkeeping and derivations remain reading. A sticking collision is one limiting model, not a universal collision rule. |
| 6. Circular motion / p.132 | Centripetal force (F = mv² / r); Angular and linear speed (v = ωr; T = 2π / ω); A frictionless banked road (v = √(rg tan θ)) | Real banked turns can involve friction. Vertical-circle minimum-speed conditions require contact constraints beyond the uniform-circle model. |
| 7. Gravitation / p.154 | Inverse-square attraction (F = Gm₁m₂ / r²); A circular Earth orbit (v = √(GM / (R Earth + h))); Escape speed (v escape = √(2GM / r)) | GPS, geostationary geometry and historical discussion stay as guided reading. Orbits assume a spherical Earth; the orbit animation compresses the time scale. |
| 8. Elasticity / p.184 | Hooke’s law (F = kx; E = ½kx²); Stretch a wire (ΔL = FL / (AY)); Stress and strain (σ = F/A; ε = σ/Y) | Plastic deformation, hysteresis and fracture require material data. The spring and wire are linear elastic models, not predictions of breaking strength. |
| 9. Heat and temperature / p.208 | Three temperature scales (K = °C + 273.15; °F = 1.8°C + 32); Fahrenheit conversion (°C = (°F − 32) × 5/9); Thermal equilibrium (T final = (C₁T₁ + C₂T₂) / (C₁ + C₂)) | Temperature is not a measure of total thermal energy. The thermometer is a scale illustration; it does not replace real thermometry. |
| 10. Thermal expansion / p.222 | Linear expansion (ΔL = αL₀ΔT); Volume expansion (ΔV ≈ 3αV₀ΔT); A constrained rod (σ = YαΔT) | Pullinger’s apparatus and balanced-column experiments remain practical activities. First-order expansion neglects higher powers of the small fractional change. |
| 11. Quantity of heat / p.246 | Heating a substance (Q = mcΔT); Melting ice (Q = mL fusion); Newton’s law of cooling (T(t) = T ambient + (T₀ − T ambient)e⁻ᵏᵗ) | Real evaporation, pressure-dependent phase diagrams and calorimeter calibration need experimental data. Phase-change labs use water at standard pressure. |
| 12. Rate of heat flow / p.270 | Heat through a wall (P = kAΔT / L); Net thermal radiation (P = εσA(T⁴ − T surroundings⁴)); Blackbody peak (λ peak = b / T) | Convection is illustrated rather than solved as a fluid simulation. Searle’s apparatus requires real measurement. Radiation models assume a grey surface with constant emissivity. |
| 13. Ideal gas / p.289 | Pressure, volume, temperature (P = nRT / V); Molecular speed (v rms = √(3RT / M)); Molecular kinetic energy (⟨E translational⟩ = 3kBT / 2) | Particles are a qualitative display, not a molecular dynamics calculation. Real gases deviate at high density and near condensation. |
| 14. Reflection at curved mirrors / p.307 | Concave mirror images (1/f = 1/u + 1/v; m = −v/u); Convex mirror images (v = fu/(u − f), with f < 0); Curvature and focus (f = R/2) | The diagram uses paraxial rays, not spherical aberration. This lab uses the real-is-positive convention and states it explicitly; compare with the sign convention on the source page. |
| 15. Refraction at plane surfaces / p.319 | Snell’s law (n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r); Critical angle (c = sin⁻¹(n₂/n₁), for n₁ > n₂); Apparent depth (Apparent depth = real depth × n observer / n medium) | Wave derivations and optical-fibre applications stay as reading. Ray models neglect reflection amplitudes and wave interference. |
| 16. Refraction through prisms / p.336 | Trace through a prism (r₁ = asin(sin i/n); r₂ = A − r₁; δ = i + e − A); Minimum deviation (δ min = 2 asin(n sin(A/2)) − A); A thin prism (δ ≈ (n − 1)A) | Prism measurements and spectrometer alignment remain practical tasks. The ray tracer reports when the second face causes total internal reflection. |
| 17. Lenses / p.345 | A converging lens (1/f = 1/u + 1/v; m = −v/u); A diverging lens (v = fu/(u − f), with f < 0); Lenses in contact (P total = P₁ + P₂; f = 1/P total) | Thick-lens effects, visual-angle experiments and aberrations are outside the thin-lens model. The lab declares a real-is-positive convention to keep signs consistent. |
| 18. Dispersion / p.364 | Separate red and violet (Angular separation ≈ (n violet − n red)A); Dispersive power (ω = (n violet − n red)/(n yellow − 1)); An achromatic doublet (ω₁P₁ + ω₂P₂ = 0; P₂ = −ω₁P₁/ω₂) | Colour bands are illustrative, not a calibrated spectrum. Lens aberration needs wavelength-dependent material data for quantitative prediction. |
| 19. Electric charges / p.378 | Two electric charges (F signed = kq₁q₂ / r²); Charge in electron units (Q = −Ne); Charges in a dielectric (F signed = kq₁q₂/(εᵣr²)) | Charging by friction and induction are guided conceptual activities, not material-specific electron-transfer predictions. |
| 20. Electric field / p.387 | Field of a point charge (E radial = kQ / r²); Uniform field between plates (E = V/d); Flux through a flat surface (Φ = EA cos θ) | Field lines and flux surfaces are representations. Gauss’s law requires symmetry to extract a field magnitude easily; irregular charge distributions need numerical solvers. |
| 21. Electric potential & energy / p.403 | Potential of a point charge (V = kQ/r); Energy of a charge (U = qV); Potential gradient (Eₓ = −ΔV/Δx) | Potential is defined relative to a reference. The point-charge model takes zero at infinity and excludes the charge’s singular position. |
| 22. Capacitors / p.416 | Build a capacitor (C = ε₀εᵣA/d); Stored electrical energy (U = ½CV²); Capacitors in series (C equivalent = C₁C₂/(C₁ + C₂)) | Dielectric breakdown and fringing require material and geometry data. The model keeps ideal fixed capacitance and never predicts a safe operating voltage. |
| 23. D.C. circuits / p.431 | Voltage, resistance & current (I = V/R; P = VI); Resistors in parallel (R equivalent = R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂)); A real cell (I = ℰ/(R + r); V terminal = ℰ − Ir) | Non-ohmic curves and real-cell chemistry stay as reading. Circuit labs are ideal DC calculations; they are not a general circuit solver. |
| 24. Nuclear physics / p.459 | Mass defect and binding (E binding = Δm × 931.494 MeV/u); Size of a nucleus (R ≈ r₀A¹ᐟ³); Mass into energy (E = mc²) | Scattering, fission and fusion use conceptual representations. The lab is not a reactor or microscopic nuclear-dynamics simulation. Mass inputs must consistently use either nuclear or atomic conventions. |
| 25. Energy levels / p.487 | Hydrogen energy levels (Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV); Emit a photon (ΔE = 13.6(1/n lower² − 1/n upper²); λ = hc/ΔE); Semiconductor dopants (N dopant = fraction × N atoms) | Electron orbits are not literal classical tracks. The hydrogen model is idealized; semiconductor carrier displays do not solve a real junction. Source chapter headings are retained. |
| 26. Solids · particles & cosmology / p.496 | Build proton or neutron (Q/e = (2N up − N down)/3; N up + N down = 3); The expanding universe (v recession ≈ H₀d); Cosmic wavelength shift (z = (λ observed − λ emitted)/λ emitted) | Particle properties are learning models, not simulated collisions. The expansion analogy is schematic; Hubble’s linear law is for modest redshift, and dark matter and gravitational-wave discussion remain reading. |

## Exercises

78 randomized numeric exercise generators share the lab equations and use frozen parameters. Answers accept scientific notation, a 1% relative or 0.01 absolute tolerance (whichever is larger), plus explicit infinity/no-ray cases. Hints and worked substitutions are available. 26 original conceptual MCQs provide explained feedback. The source exercise notebook includes extracted question cards, student notes, printed-answer reveals where extraction succeeds, and self-assessment. These source cards are not automatically graded. Figures, broken equations and printed answers must be checked in the linked original PDF. No independent verification of printed source keys is implied.

## What remains reading or practical

Definitions, historical notes, proofs and derivations remain readable; a simulation does not prove a law. Physical calibration, apparatus handling, fracture, hysteresis, detailed fluid convection, real-gas behaviour, lens aberrations, semiconductor transport, nuclear dynamics and general-relativistic cosmology require data or more advanced models. The elementary models state their assumptions. All source chapters remain available in the reader and PDF. Chapter 25 also covers semiconductors; Chapter 26 is titled Solids but contains particles/cosmology.

## Delivery and verification

Self-contained static site with bundled dependencies and source PDF. Search, chapter navigation, source reading, lab/practice tabs, progress and source notes (stored locally in the browser), pause/restart, parameter comparison and adjustable response graphs. Numerical models, parameter endpoints and singular cases are checked programmatically. Canvas API smoke checks cover all laboratories. Supported browser visual QA is unavailable in this session; report that limit.

## React and direct manipulation update

The interface now uses React 19 components and hooks. Pointer-captured SVG controls share Canvas coordinates and update the same parameters as numerical controls, equations, feedback and response graphs. Drag support covers vector tips, projectile velocity, spring masses, optical object distances, refraction incidence, charge separation, torque levers, capacitor plate spacing and electric flux normals. Mouse, touch and keyboard controls are supported.

A separate mass drop sandbox (`#drop`) supports lifting and releasing a mass from rest. It follows h = h₀ − ½gt², v = gt, PE = mgh and KE = ½mv², terminating at ground contact. Mass changes energy while height and gravity determine fall time. It omits drag, rebounds and impact dynamics. Other laboratories retain linked parameter controls rather than arbitrary object dragging.

## Expanded animation replay

Additional motion is implemented in Newton acceleration, incline friction, work along a prescribed displacement, energy during uniform acceleration, sticking collisions, cooling, conduction/radiation, four lens/mirror models, refraction/critical-angle paths and photon emission (15 labs). Animated labs have playback speeds and a scrubber. Quantitative current-state captions distinguish replay values from selected-parameter answers. Heat and ray marker speeds are schematic; cooling is time compressed; collisions use a centre-of-mass view; quantum emission is a discrete state sequence. Zero net drive remains stationary.


## Electricity flow and RC sandbox

Ohm, parallel-resistor and cell circuits show conventional current or reverse electron drift in conducting leads. Marker speed is proportional to current; parallel branches carry their own currents and shared leads carry their sum. The master switch disconnects both branches. Open switches and zero driving voltage stop flow; resistor shading follows load power. The response graph and captured baseline continue to compare closed-circuit parameters. Electron motion and marker spacing are schematic, not measured drift velocities or signal propagation.

The React RC sandbox at `#charge` models charging from zero and discharging from the selected initial voltage with the source removed. It shows equal and opposite plate charge, capacitor voltage, current magnitude, stored energy, resistor heat rate, and exponential voltage/current graphs. Charges do not cross the capacitor gap. Play, pause, restart, speed, timeline seeking and a one-time-constant shortcut are supported. Five physical time constants are scaled to eight playback seconds; the run stops at 5τ. R and C change the physical time scale. No stray capacitance, inductance, leakage, dielectric breakdown, or microscopic electron dynamics are modeled.

`electricity.mjs` holds the DC/RC models and circuit marker geometry; `electrical.jsx` renders the RC sandbox. `electricity-tests.mjs` verifies branch-current sums, cell power balance, RC exponential values and energy balance, current-proportional marker speed, reverse electron direction and zero-flow cases. Mounted React tests verify switch results, capacitor motion, pause, seek, reset, parameter changes, zero voltage, automatic stopping and unmount cleanup. Browser visual QA remains unavailable.


## Optical shapes and image formation

Converging/diverging lenses now have convex/concave glass silhouettes; curved mirrors show concave/convex reflecting surfaces. The outlines are schematic and do not infer curvature from focal length. Thin lenses in contact show two signed-power lens shapes. Existing ray equations, object dragging and quantitative models remain linked.

A picture panel in lens, mirror and apparent-depth labs displays an asymmetrical sample image, or a browser-local PNG/JPEG/WebP upload up to 5 MB. Signed magnification drives image size and orientation. Virtual images are outlined; focus singularities omit a finite image. A new sandbox at `#light` compares convex and concave lenses, plane and curved mirrors, and near-normal underwater apparent depth. Plane-mirror images are equally sized and reversed. The water view shows the actual position as a ghost and raises/compresses the apparent picture according to the near-normal approximation. Uploads are not sent to a server or persisted. Phone diagrams now fit an adaptive viewBox with vertically stacked depth panels.

This is an ideal geometrical-optics illustration, not a photograph ray tracer: no blur, aberrations, Fresnel intensity, scattering or thick-lens surface tracing. `optics.mjs` contains shape and image helpers; `optical-images.jsx` provides the shared picture panel and sandbox. Tests cover signed image formation, shape geometry, plane symmetry, depth, image uploads/reset, singularities, prediction mode and all six sandbox modes. Browser visual QA remains unavailable.


## Phone and tablet layout

Phone diagrams now use matching Canvas and SVG coordinate systems rather than enlarged CSS crops. Dragging converts touch coordinates using the active viewBox. Phone response graphs use a narrower plotting area and larger text. The mass sandbox stacks expanded energy bars below the falling mass; the electricity sandbox stacks an expanded transient chart below the circuit. Optics recomputes its horizontal fit, keeps object and formed image visible, and stacks apparent-depth panels. No horizontal image panning is needed.

Inputs and sliders have larger touch targets; phone text fields use 16px to avoid automatic focus zoom. Playback controls, uploads, metrics, quizzes and chapter-plan cards stack into narrow-screen layouts. Sticky phone navigation, safe-area spacing, a tablet chapter drawer, background scroll locking, focus handling and Escape/backdrop dismissal keep navigation accessible. Browser pinch zoom remains available outside drag handles. Existing notes, progress, equations and desktop interactions are retained.

Mounted React tests verify phone viewport changes, touch-coordinate alignment for vectors and mass drops, visible stacked charts/energy/depth panels, optics picture fit, orientation changes, and drawer scroll locking. The full physics/React regression suite passes. Browser visual QA is unavailable in this environment; no device screenshots or browser layout measurements are claimed.
